**Important note:** this week is about whether an insurer may price on
sex, directly or through other variables, and about which causal paths
from a protected attribute are fair. The algebra below is not
contested. Which causal graph describes a real case, which paths are
fair, and what the law should require are contested, and my view is
one view. A well-argued position I think is wrong can still get full
marks.

## Summary

Since December 2012 an insurer in the European Union may not use sex
as a factor in its premiums. It can still use the car, the mileage and
everything else it records, and some of those depend on sex. The
observational criteria compare groups in a table, and the same table
can come from different mechanisms. This week writes the mechanism down
as a causal model, which makes a new kind of question possible: what
would this person's price have been had the attribute been different?

Counterfactual fairness asks that the answer be the same price. In the
simplest example, the red car, the price that never looks at sex fails
this test and a price that uses sex passes it. Direct and indirect
effects split the effect of an attribute along the paths it takes, and
the total effect is their sum when the two are defined with matching
reference levels. A path-specific criterion removes the effect of the
attribute only along the paths judged unfair. On one small model, the
counterfactually fair price and the path-specific price differ by the
contribution of the path someone judged fair.

Which paths are fair is not something the data can say. It is a
judgment about control and responsibility, and moral luck, the control
principle and luck egalitarianism bear on it. The week ends where those ideas meet the law: the
counterfactually fair price needs the attribute that the law forbids
an insurer to use.

```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
set.seed(313)
# cividis: viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)]
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two

# Causal graphs. Nodes are letters in circles, or words in boxes (boxes = TRUE). A node's
# size is fixed on the page, in inches; draw_dag measures the device and stops every arrow
# `gap` inches short of its nodes. From weeks 3 to 5.
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, dashed = character(0), highlight = character(0), boxes = FALSE,
                     text_size = 7, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), strip_size = 18,
                     gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  pad <- unit(0.35, "lines"); border <- 0.5; dot <- 16; stroke <- 0.8; lw <- c(black = 0.7, gold = 1.5)
  p <- ggplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = strip_size), panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
  p <- if (boxes) {
    p + geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, label.size = border,
                   label.padding = pad)
  } else {
    p + geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
      geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, parse = TRUE)
  }
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  if (boxes) {
    text <- lapply(as.character(nodes$name), grid::textGrob, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = text_size * .pt))
    nodes$hw <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobWidth(t), grid::convertWidth)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertWidth) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
    nodes$hh <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobHeight(t), grid::convertHeight)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertHeight) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  } else {
    nodes$hw <- nodes$hh <- (0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 +
                               stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  }
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |>
    rename(x0 = x, y0 = y, hw0 = hw, hh0 = hh) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(dx = x - x0, dy = y - y0, len = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2), ux = dx / len, uy = dy / len,
           col = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% highlight, "#BCAF6F", "black"),
           style = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% dashed, "dashed", "solid"),
           g0 = gap / per_unit,
           g1 = (gap + ifelse(col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]) * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           s0 = if (boxes) pmin((hw0 + g0) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh0 + g0) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw0 + g0,
           s1 = if (boxes) pmin((hw + g1) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh + g1) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw + g1,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye, linetype = style, color = col),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
                   linewidth = ifelse(e$col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_linetype_identity() + scale_color_identity()
}

# The mileage world (as in the slides). The checks stop the render if a number stated in
# the text does not follow from the parameters.
mu0 <- 10; alpha <- -4; beta <- 0.25; gamma <- -0.5; var_UM <- 4; pA <- 1/2
NDE <- gamma; NIE <- alpha * beta; TE <- NDE + NIE
var_M <- alpha^2 * pA * (1 - pA) + var_UM
slope_refit <- beta + gamma * alpha * pA * (1 - pA) / var_M
R2 <- alpha^2 * pA * (1 - pA) / var_M
stopifnot(abs(NDE + 0.5) < 1e-12, abs(NIE + 1) < 1e-12, abs(TE + 1.5) < 1e-12,
          abs(var_M - 8) < 1e-12, abs(slope_refit - 0.3125) < 1e-12, abs(R2 - 0.5) < 1e-12,
          abs(alpha * slope_refit - (NIE + R2 * NDE)) < 1e-12)
```

## What you brought

The task was to bring one decision in which an attribute is used, or
deliberately not used, with one route by which it could affect the
outcome, and whether that route is fair. A route is a path in a causal
graph: an arrow from the attribute to something, and on to the
outcome. Drawing it makes the judgment visible, because the judgment
is always about a particular arrow. "Sex affects the premium" says
little; "sex affects how many miles a person drives, and mileage
affects claims" names a path someone can defend or object to.

## The red car

### Pricing without sex

On 1 March 2011 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled on a
question sent to it by the Belgian Constitutional Court, where
Test-Achats, a Belgian consumers' association, had challenged the
Belgian law transposing an EU directive that prohibits discrimination
based on sex in access to goods and services. The directive prohibited
the use of sex as a factor in insurance premiums and benefits, but let
member states allow exceptions, provided the actuarial and statistical
data behind them were reliable, regularly updated and available to the
public. The Court's press release is headed "Taking the gender
of the insured individual into account as a risk factor in insurance
contracts constitutes discrimination", and the Court ruled that the
exception was invalid from 21 December 2012. Since then, insurers in
the EU may not use sex as a factor in premiums and benefits.

The law forbids an input. It does not forbid predicting claims from
everything else, and some of everything else depends on sex. The
observational criteria cannot say whether that is fair, because the
same table of counts can come from different mechanisms. The mechanism
has to be written down.

### The red car

[ms4ds, section 3.4.1](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#causal-models),
and Kusner, Loftus, Russell and Silva (2017), the first of whose
scenarios this is, describe an insurer that predicts the accident
rate or the claims $Y$ of a policy from the color of the car $X$. An
unobserved factor $U$, aggressive driving, makes a person both more
likely to choose a red car and more likely to have an accident.
Members of one group, $A = 1$, are more likely to drive red cars, and
no more likely to be aggressive or to have accidents. Kusner et al.
take $A$ to be race; ms4ds takes it to be gender, and so do these
notes, with $A = 1$ for a woman.

```{r dag_redcar, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=1.6, fig.width=7, fig.alt="A causal graph in boxes: A, sex, points into X, car color; U, aggression, points into X and into Y, claims. There is no arrow from A to U or from A to Y."}
rc <- data.frame(name = c("A: sex", "X: car color", "U: aggression", "Y: claims"),
                 x = c(0, 1.25, 2.5, 3.75), y = c(1, 0, 1, 0))
draw_dag(rc, data.frame(from = c("A: sex", "U: aggression", "U: aggression"),
                        to = c("X: car color", "X: car color", "Y: claims")),
         boxes = TRUE, text_size = 4.5, xlim = c(-0.75, 4.5), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3))
```

The graph is $A \to X \leftarrow U \to Y$. There is no directed path
from $A$ to $Y$: sex has no effect on claims. The insurer, forbidden to
use sex, predicts from the car alone. ms4ds calls this *functional
independence*, $\hat Y = \hat f(X)$ with $A$ not an input; Kusner et al.
call it *fairness through unawareness*.

### The unaware price

Take a linear version with numbers. Half the drivers are women, so
$A \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1/2)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(A) = 1/4$;
$U \sim N(0, 1)$, independent of $A$; car color on a continuous scale,
higher for redder, is $X = 2A + U$; and claims are $Y = U + \varepsilon$,
with $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1)$ independent of $(A, U)$.

The test-score model from the discussion of leaving a column out had
the same shape with $Y$ in the place of $U$: $X = Y + 2A + \varepsilon$.
There, the model that could not use $A$ read group 1's two coached
points as ability and predicted group 1 higher. The same happens here.
The least-squares slope of $Y$ on $X$ alone is

$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(U)}{2^2 \operatorname{Var}(A) + \operatorname{Var}(U)}
= \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac12 ,
$$

and since $E[X] = 1$ and $E[Y] = 0$, the fitted line is
$\hat Y = \tfrac12 X - \tfrac12$. Women's average car color is $2$ and
men's is $0$, so women's average predicted claims are $\tfrac12$ and
men's are $-\tfrac12$. Average claims are $0$ in both groups. The price
that never looks at sex charges women more, for claims they do not
make.

A simulation of 1,000 drivers, and least squares with and without $A$:

```{r redcar_sim}
n <- 1000
A <- rbinom(n, 1, 1/2)          # 1 for a woman
U <- rnorm(n)                   # aggression, never observed
X <- 2 * A + U                  # car color
Y <- U + rnorm(n)               # claims
coef(lm(Y ~ X))                 # the price from X alone
coef(lm(Y ~ X + A))             # the price from X and A
```

```{r redcar_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Scatter plot of claims Y against car color X for 1,000 simulated drivers, men in navy and women in gold, the gold cloud shifted two units right. A dashed black line of slope one half runs through both clouds; a navy line Y = X and a gold line Y = X - 2 run through the men's and the women's clouds."}
car <- data.frame(X, Y, group = factor(A, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("men", "women")))
ggplot(car, aes(X, Y, color = group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 0.9) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = navy, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -2, slope = 1, color = gold, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -1/2, slope = 1/2, color = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "X: car color (higher is redder)", y = "Y: claims") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3)))
```

The figure shows the simulated drivers and the population lines. The
dashed line is the fit on $X$ alone. The two solid lines are the best
predictions from $X$ and $A$, one for each group: at any given color, a
woman has lower expected claims than a man.

### A counterfactual driver

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
A woman's car scores $X = 2.6$. What would her price from $X$ alone have
been, had she been a man? Write down how you got there.
:::

The reading's Definition 5 (page 123) gives three steps for a
counterfactual in a structural causal model. *Abduction*: adjust the
unobserved variables to be consistent with what was observed. Here
$U = X - 2A = 0.6$. *Action*: set the attribute, $A := 0$.
*Prediction*: recompute everything downstream of $A$ in the modified
model, with the abducted $U$. Her car would have scored
$X = 2 \cdot 0 + 0.6 = 0.6$: two units of her color came from $A$
rather than from $U$.

| | she, $A = 1$ | had $A$ been $0$ |
|:---|---:|---:|
| abduction: $U = X - 2A$ | $0.6$ | $0.6$ |
| prediction: $X = 2A + U$ | $2.6$ | $0.6$ |
| price from $X$ alone, $\tfrac12 X - \tfrac12$ | $0.8$ | $-0.2$ |
| price from $X$ and $A$, $X - 2A$ | $0.6$ | $0.6$ |

The unaware price for this driver would have been one unit lower had
she been a man. The price that uses $A$, which is the best prediction
from $X$ and $A$ in this model, would have been the same.

### Counterfactual fairness

Write $\hat Y(a)$ for the prediction for the same person, with $U$
abducted from what was observed about them, had $A$ been set to $a$.
Kusner et al. write $\hat Y_{A \leftarrow a}(U)$; the reading writes
$\hat Y_{A := a}(E)$, with $E$ the observed event.

**Counterfactual fairness** (Kusner et al., Definition 5, page 3). A
predictor $\hat Y$ is counterfactually fair if, for every $x$ and $a$,
and every value $a'$ of $A$,

$$
P\big(\hat Y(a) = y \mid X = x, A = a\big) = P\big(\hat Y(a') = y \mid X = x, A = a\big) \quad \text{for all } y .
$$

The distribution is over the values of $U$ consistent with what was
observed; in the red car, $U$ is determined by $X$ and $A$, so it is a
single value. Kusner et al. call this "an individual-level definition"
(page 3): it compares a person with themselves, not one group with
another. The reading calls the same condition counterfactual
demographic parity (page 129).

**Lemma 1** (Kusner et al., page 5). If $\hat Y$ is a function of the
non-descendants of $A$ in the causal graph, it is counterfactually
fair. A non-descendant of $A$ takes the same value whatever $A$ is set
to, so any function of non-descendants does too. Kusner et al. add that
a predictor can use descendants of $A$ and still be counterfactually
fair, but only where the dependence on $A$ cancels, which does not
happen in general.

**The red car, linear.** Let $X = \beta_A A + U$ and $Y = U + \varepsilon$
with $\beta_A \neq 0$, $U$ and $\varepsilon$ independent of $A$ and of
each other. The least-squares predictor from $X$ alone is
$\hat Y = \lambda X + \lambda_0$ with
$\lambda = \operatorname{Var}(U) / (\beta_A^2 \operatorname{Var}(A) + \operatorname{Var}(U)) > 0$.
For the same $U$, $X(a) - X(a') = \beta_A (a - a')$, so
$\hat Y(a) - \hat Y(a') = \lambda \beta_A (a - a') \neq 0$: the unaware
predictor is not counterfactually fair. The least-squares predictor
from $X$ and $A$ is $E[Y \mid X, A] = X - \beta_A A$, because $U$ is
determined by $(X, A)$; and $X - \beta_A A = U$, a non-descendant of
$A$, so by Lemma 1 it is counterfactually fair. With $\beta_A = 2$
these are the two prices in the table. Kusner et al. prove the same
statement as Lemma 3 of their supplement (page 14), and say it in a
sentence on page 4: "Regressing Y on X alone obeys the FTU criterion but
is not counterfactually fair, so omitting A (FTU) may introduce
unfairness into an otherwise fair world." The counterfactually fair
price uses the attribute; the price that ignores it does not satisfy
the definition.

This depends on the model. The fair predictor is built from $U$, and
$U$ is never observed: it is abducted from $X$ and $A$ through the
structural equation for $X$. A different model for $X$ gives a
different $U$, and a different fair price. Kusner et al. describe three
levels of assumption (page 7). Using only the observed non-descendants
of $A$ needs least; using the error terms of an additive model, as
here, extracts the most information and assumes the most.

### Conditioning or intervening

In this world $P(Y \mid do(A := 1)) = P(Y \mid do(A := 0))$: there is
no directed path from $A$ to $Y$. Yet in the fitted
$\hat Y = X - 2A$ the coefficient on $A$ is $-2$. The coefficient
compares women and men with the same car color. Car color is a
collider on the path $A \to X \leftarrow U$, and among drivers with
the same $X$, a woman's color owes two units to $A$, so her $U$ is two
units lower. The coefficient is a statement about conditioning on $X$;
the absence of an effect is a statement about intervening on $A$.

## Direct and indirect effects

### A second world

The red car has no path from $A$ to $Y$ at all. In most cases that
matter, the attribute does affect the outcome, along some paths that
people find acceptable and some that they do not. Keep the insurer and
change the world. Annual mileage $M$, in thousands of miles, depends on
sex, and claims $Y$, in hundreds of pounds a year, depend on mileage
and on sex directly:

$$
M = \mu_0 + \alpha A + U_M, \qquad Y = \gamma A + \beta M + U_Y ,
$$

with $U_M$ and $U_Y$ of mean zero, independent of each other and of
$A$, and $A = 1$ for a woman. The numbers are invented for the
arithmetic: $\mu_0 = 10$, $\alpha = -4$, $\beta = 0.25$,
$\gamma = -0.5$. Men drive $10{,}000$ miles a year on average and women
$6{,}000$; each thousand miles adds £25 a year in expected claims; and
at the same mileage, women's expected claims are £50 a year lower.

```{r dag_mileage, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=1.6, fig.width=7, fig.alt="A causal graph in boxes: A, sex, points into M, mileage, and into Y, claims; M points into Y."}
mw <- data.frame(name = c("A: sex", "M: mileage", "Y: claims"), x = c(0, 1.6, 3.2), y = c(0, 1, 0))
draw_dag(mw, data.frame(from = c("A: sex", "M: mileage", "A: sex"), to = c("M: mileage", "Y: claims", "Y: claims")),
         boxes = TRUE, text_size = 4.5, xlim = c(-0.7, 3.9), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3))
```

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
Sex affects claims here directly and through mileage. For one person,
how would you define the part of the effect of sex on claims that does
not go through mileage?
:::

### Counterfactuals with a mediator

A natural first answer is to compare a woman and a man at the same
mileage. Making that precise, and the alternative to it, needs two kinds
of counterfactual, both built from $do(\cdot)$:

- $Y(a, m)$, the claims under $do(A := a, M := m)$;
- $M(a)$, the mileage under $do(A := a)$.

Combining them, $Y(a, M(a'))$ is the claims with $A$ set to $a$ and
mileage set to the value it would have taken under $A = a'$. When
$a \neq a'$ this is a cross-world quantity: $Y(1, M(0))$ is a woman
driving the miles she would have driven as a man. Nobody's data
contain it. The reading writes $Y_{X := 1,\, Z := Z_{X := 0}}$ for the
same thing, with $X$ the treatment and $Z$ the mediator (pages 127 and
128); these notes keep $Z$ for a confounder and $X$ for covariates.

The **controlled direct effect** at mileage $m$ sets the mediator to
the same value for everyone:
$\text{CDE}(m) = E[Y(1, m) - Y(0, m)]$. It needs only $do(\cdot)$.

### The decomposition

The **total effect** is $\text{TE} = E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))]$, the
same as $E[Y \mid do(A := 1)] - E[Y \mid do(A := 0)]$. Add and subtract
$E[Y(1, M(0))]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{TE} &= E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))] \\
&= \underbrace{E[Y(1, M(0)) - Y(0, M(0))]}_{\text{NDE}} \\
&\quad + \underbrace{E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0))]}_{\text{NIE}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The **natural direct effect** changes $A$ with mileage held at the value
it would have taken under $A = 0$. The **natural indirect effect** holds
$A$ at $1$ and changes mileage from $M(0)$ to $M(1)$. No model was used,
so $\text{TE} = \text{NDE} + \text{NIE}$ in any model where the
expectations exist, provided the NIE holds $A$ at the level the NDE
moves it to.

The reading defines the natural indirect effect with $A$ held at $0$,
$E[Y(0, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))]$ (page 128). With that definition the sum
of the two natural effects is the total effect only in models where
the indirect effect does not depend on the level at which $A$ is held,
such as the linear model below. With an interaction between $A$ and
$M$ the two can differ.

The natural effects need more than $do(\cdot)$: they combine two
settings of $A$ for the same person, which no experiment can do.
Estimating them from data needs an assumption about the two worlds
together. In the model above it is built in, by taking $U_M$ and $U_Y$
independent; with no confounding of $A$ and $M$ or $M$ and $Y$, the
reading gives the indirect effect as a formula in conditional
expectations (page 128).

### In the linear model

Put the structural equations into the definitions:

$$
M(a) = \mu_0 + \alpha a + U_M, \qquad Y(a, m) = \gamma a + \beta m + U_Y .
$$

Then $Y(1, m) - Y(0, m) = \gamma$ for every $m$, so
$\text{CDE}(m) = \gamma$. The NDE holds mileage at $M(0)$ in both
terms, so it is also $\gamma$. In the NIE,
$Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0)) = \beta\,(M(1) - M(0)) = \alpha\beta$: the
same $U_M$ appears in $M(1)$ and $M(0)$ and cancels. So

$$
\text{CDE}(m) = \text{NDE} = \gamma, \qquad
\text{NIE} = \alpha\beta, \qquad
\text{TE} = \gamma + \alpha\beta .
$$

In a linear model with no interaction, the indirect effect is the
product of the coefficients along the path. In the mileage world,
$\text{NDE} = -0.5$, $\text{NIE} = -4 \times 0.25 = -1$ and
$\text{TE} = -1.5$: women's expected claims are £150 a year lower than
men's, £100 of it through mileage and £50 directly.

### Holding a mediator fixed

$Y(1, M(0))$ is nobody's observed outcome; the model supplies it, and
every statement about the natural direct effect is a statement about
the model.

A regression of $Y$ on $A$ and $M$ compares women and men with the same
mileage. In the model above, its coefficient on $A$ is $\gamma$, the
controlled direct effect, because nothing else affects both mileage and
claims. Suppose something does: driving for work, $U$, adds miles and,
mile for mile, adds claims. Then $M$ is a collider on the path
$A \to M \leftarrow U \to Y$. Women drive fewer miles on average, so a
woman with the same mileage as a man is more likely to drive for work,
and at equal mileage her expected claims are higher, relative to his,
than the direct effect alone would make them: the coefficient on $A$
lies above $\gamma$. Comparing people with the same
value of a mediator holds it fixed in the data, which is not the same
as holding it fixed by intervention.

## Two fair predictors

Before December 2012 the insurer's best prediction was the full one,
$\hat Y_{\text{full}} = \gamma A + \beta M$, which is $E[Y \mid A, M]$ in
this world.

::: {.callout-note .ask icon=false title="Before reading on, try this"}
Starting from $\hat Y_{\text{full}} = \gamma A + \beta M$, write down a
premium that removes the effect of sex along every path from $A$. Then
write down one that removes it along $A \to Y$ only, and keeps the path
through mileage.
:::

The first is the counterfactually fair premium and the second the
path-specific one. On this model both can be computed by hand.

### The counterfactually fair premium

Abduction: $U_M = M - \mu_0 - \alpha A$. Action: $A := 0$ along every
path. Prediction: mileage would have been $M(0) = \mu_0 + U_M =
M - \alpha A$, and the premium

$$
\hat Y_{\text{CF}} = \gamma \cdot 0 + \beta\, M(0) = \beta\,(M - \alpha A) = \beta\,(\mu_0 + U_M) .
$$

It is a function of $U_M$ alone, and $U_M$ is not a descendant of $A$,
so it is counterfactually fair by Lemma 1. It takes $A$ as an input:
with $\alpha = -4$, a woman is priced as if she drove $4{,}000$ more
miles than she does. Every driver, woman or man, is priced as the full
model would price the same person had they been a man, so the average
premium is the same in both groups.

### The path-specific premium

Chiappa (2019, page 7801) defines path-specific counterfactual fairness:
"a decision is fair toward an individual if it coincides with the one
that would have been taken in a counterfactual world in which the
sensitive attribute along the unfair pathways were different." Nabi and
Shpitser (2018) define discrimination as the effect of $A$ along the
paths judged unfair, a path-specific effect, and fit models in which it
is held near zero.

Suppose the direct arrow $A \to Y$ is judged unfair and the path
through mileage fair. Set $A := 0$ along the direct arrow only, and keep
the mileage the person drives:

$$
\hat Y_{\text{PS}} = \gamma \cdot 0 + \beta M = \beta M .
$$

It does not use $A$ at all, and women, who drive less, pay less on
average.

### The comparison

```{r premiums, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Dot chart of average premiums in hundreds of pounds a year. Full prediction: men 2.5, women 1.0. Path-specific: men 2.5, women 1.5. Counterfactually fair: men 2.5, women 2.5."}
prem <- data.frame(
  predictor = rep(c("full", "path-specific", "counterfactually fair"), each = 2),
  group = rep(c("men", "women"), 3),
  mean = c(beta * mu0, gamma + beta * (mu0 + alpha), beta * mu0, beta * (mu0 + alpha), beta * mu0, beta * mu0))
lev <- c("counterfactually fair", "path-specific", "full")
prem |>
  mutate(row = match(predictor, lev), y = row + ifelse(group == "women", 0.14, -0.14)) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, y, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = mean + ifelse(group == "women", -0.14, 0.14), label = sprintf("%.1f", mean)),
            size = 4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.7, 2.9), breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = lev, limits = c(0.6, 3.4)) +
  labs(x = "average premium, hundreds of pounds a year", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

| premium | formula | men | women | gap |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| full | $\gamma A + \beta M$ | $2.5$ | $1.0$ | $-1.5$, the TE |
| path-specific | $\beta M$ | $2.5$ | $1.5$ | $-1$, the NIE |
| counterfactually fair | $\beta(M - \alpha A)$ | $2.5$ | $2.5$ | $0$ |

The three differ, for every driver, by

$$
\hat Y_{\text{full}} - \hat Y_{\text{PS}} = \gamma A, \qquad
\hat Y_{\text{PS}} - \hat Y_{\text{CF}} = \alpha\beta A .
$$

The first difference is the contribution of the direct path, and the
second is the contribution of the path through mileage. The two fair
premiums differ by the contribution of the path someone judged fair.
Neither criterion says which path that is.

### The baseline

The counterfactually fair premium above prices everyone as the full
model would price them had they been men. Pricing everyone as the full
model would price them had they been women,
$\gamma + \beta(\mu_0 + \alpha + U_M)$, is also a function of $U_M$ and
also counterfactually fair, at a lower level for everyone.
So is either one plus a constant. The definition fixes the gap between
groups at zero and leaves the level open. An insurer whose premiums
must cover its average claims has to choose
a level, and at that level women pay on average more than they claim,
and men less. Which group is the baseline, and what level is
charged, are further choices the definition does not make.

### Whose judgment

The criteria need a list of fair and unfair paths, and the sources are
explicit that the list comes from outside the data.

Kusner et al.'s supplementary material (page 15) adapts the Berkeley
admissions example, with $A$ an indicator of a female applicant and
$X$ the course applied to: "Our judgment is that the higher
rejection among female than male applicants is acceptable, if the
mechanism A → X is interpreted as a choice which is under the control
of the applicant."

The reading, on the same example, says that treating department choice
as the applicant's own inherent preference "is a substantive judgment
that may not be a fact" (page 119). It describes worlds consistent with
the same data in which discrimination runs through department
choice: a program advertised in a way that discouraged women
from applying, or a department known for hostility to women. Accepting
the path as fair asserts that all of these are implausible.

Nabi and Shpitser: "The specific paths which correspond to
discrimination are a domain specific issue." Their example is a
physical fitness test, which may be appropriate for a job in
construction and not for one in accounting, so that the same path from
gender through the test to hiring may or may not be discriminatory
(arXiv version, page 4).

ms4ds draws a related distinction between a shallow counterfactual and
a deep one
([section 3.4.1.1](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#counterfactual-fairness)).
A shallow counterfactual changes the name on an application and keeps
everything else in the person's life the same; a deep one asks how the
application would differ had the person had that name all their life.
The counterfactually fair premium is a deep counterfactual along every
path; the path-specific premium is deep along some paths and shallow
along the others.

### Dropping the attribute and refitting

An insurer that may not use $A$ can refit claims on mileage alone. The
least-squares slope is
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y, M) / \operatorname{Var}(M)$, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y, M) = \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(A, M) + \beta \operatorname{Var}(M)$,
so

$$
\text{slope} = \beta + \gamma\,\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(A, M)}{\operatorname{Var}(M)} ,
$$

with $\operatorname{Cov}(A, M) = \alpha \operatorname{Var}(A)$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(M) = \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(A) + \operatorname{Var}(U_M)$.

The refitted premium's gap between women and men is the slope times
$E[M \mid A = 1] - E[M \mid A = 0] = \alpha$:

$$
\alpha\beta + \gamma\,\frac{\alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(A)}{\operatorname{Var}(M)}
= \text{NIE} + R^2\,\text{NDE} ,
$$

where $R^2 = \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(A)/\operatorname{Var}(M)$ is the
share of the variance of mileage explained by sex. With
$\operatorname{Var}(A) = 1/4$ and $\operatorname{Var}(U_M) = 4$,
$\operatorname{Var}(M) = 8$, $\operatorname{Cov}(A, M) = -1$, the slope is
$0.25 + (-0.5)(-1)/8 = 0.3125$ and the gap is $-1.25$: the path through
mileage, $-1$, and half of the direct effect, $-0.25$, which returns
because mileage stands in for sex. The refitted premium has no arrow from
$A$, and charges more per mile than the world does.

Nabi and Shpitser's method fits the model closest to the data, by
likelihood, among those in which the path-specific effect judged unfair
is held within bounds. When the outcome model is linear and the
unfair effect is the natural direct effect, they note that holding it
at zero "coincides to simply dropping A from the outcome regression"
(arXiv version, page 6). In the mileage world that fitted model charges
$0.3125$ per thousand miles, and has no direct effect by construction.
Measured against the world the data came from, its gap includes half
of the direct effect. The path-specific premium $\beta M$ charges the
world's price per mile, $0.25$, and needs $\beta$, which can be
estimated only from a model that includes $A$. Which of the two is the
fair price of a mile depends on whether the fitted model or the world
is what the criterion is about.

### With an interaction

The decomposition of the total effect is an identity, and with an
interaction the natural effects in it depend on their reference
levels. Let

$$
M = \mu_0 + \alpha A + U_M, \qquad Y = \gamma A + \beta M + \delta A M + U_Y ,
$$

and write $\text{NDE}_a$ for the natural direct effect with mileage
held at $M(a)$, and $\text{NIE}_a$ for the natural indirect effect with
$A$ held at $a$. Since $E[M(0)] = \mu_0$ and $E[M(1)] = \mu_0 + \alpha$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{TE} &= \gamma + \alpha\beta + \delta(\mu_0 + \alpha) \\
\text{NDE}_0 &= E[Y(1, M(0)) - Y(0, M(0))] = \gamma + \delta\mu_0 \\
\text{NIE}_1 &= E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0))] = \alpha(\beta + \delta) \\
\text{NDE}_1 &= E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(1))] = \gamma + \delta(\mu_0 + \alpha) \\
\text{NIE}_0 &= E[Y(0, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))] = \alpha\beta .
\end{aligned}
$$

Both $\text{NDE}_0 + \text{NIE}_1$ and $\text{NDE}_1 + \text{NIE}_0$ equal
the total effect: the decomposition holds with the reference levels
paired this way, and not in general. The pair the reading defines,
$\text{NDE}_0$ and $\text{NIE}_0$, sums to $\text{TE} - \alpha\delta$.
The product of coefficients $\alpha\beta$ is $\text{NIE}_0$, which is
not the indirect effect that pairs with $\text{NDE}_0$. With
$\delta = 0$ both pairings give $\gamma$ and $\alpha\beta$.

## Luck and responsibility

### Moral luck

[ms4ds, section 3.4.2](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#moral-luck):
"Moral luck refers to how our evaluation of whether someone has done
good or not can depend on factors which are outside of that person's
control. The control principle says that we should only judge people
to the extent that the factors we judge them on are under their
control." The same section gives the control principle as one
justification for treating attributes such as race or gender as
sensitive in the first place: they are commonly understood to be
outside a person's control.

The book's middle view of equality of opportunity discounts
differences in qualifications that come from factors outside a
person's control, and the book names insurance as a case: "The middle view has particular
purchase in the case of insurance, where we really might want insurers
to ignore the additional costs that they are likely to face in setting
the price of a policy for someone with an expensive pre-existing
condition outside the person's control" (chapter 4, page 85).

### Luck egalitarianism

Luck egalitarianism applies a similar idea to who gets what. Kasper
Lippert-Rasmussen's encyclopedia entry opens with the observation that
some people end up worse off than others partly because of bad luck,
and its section 7 sets out the distinction between brute luck, risks a
person did not choose to take, and option luck, how a gamble the person
chose turns out: "Luck-egalitarians, for example, often separate option
luck and brute luck and deny that instances of differential option luck
are unjust." The entry also records that views on option luck differ:
whether justice requires its effects to stand, permits correcting them,
or requires correcting some of them.

Moral luck and luck egalitarianism are distinct ideas. Moral luck is about whether luck should
bear on how we judge what people did; luck egalitarianism is about how
goods and burdens should be distributed. This course takes them
together, because both ask what a person is responsible for, and both
answer that what a person does not control should not count against
them. A premium is a burden distributed among policyholders.

The reading marks the limit of the formal tools here: "many of the
concepts in this chapter, such as whether a decision subject has
control over an attribute used for decision making, cannot be
expressed in the statistical language of conditional probabilities and
expectations" (chapter 4, page 92). A causal graph does not settle it
either. It can show that a path exists; whether the person controls
what happens along it is the judgment that decides whether the path is
fair.

### A mediator shaped by the attribute

Mileage is a rating factor with an obvious connection to risk: more
miles, more exposure. In the mileage world it also differs by sex, and
part of what makes women's claims lower runs through it. Whether the
path $A \to M \to Y$ is fair depends on why mileage differs. If the
difference reflects choices people control, the control principle
counts the path as fair. If it reflects who does which job, or which
share of caring, it is less clear that the choice was the person's.
The Berkeley example has the same shape, with department choice in the
place of mileage, and the reading's alternative worlds are the
argument that a mediator's appearing to be a choice does not make it
one.

### A framework and a criterion

ms4ds, after showing what the unaware model does in the red car world:
"But there may be a deontological argument in favor of functional
independence, including empirical evidence that people generally
believe a process with functional independence is more fair"
([section 3.4.1](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#causal-models)).
A deontologist may hold that a decision should not take a protected
attribute as an input, whatever the consequences. In the red car world
that rule produces the price that is not counterfactually fair, and the
counterfactually fair price breaks it. Since December 2012, EU law
forbids the second. Whether a framework implies a criterion, and
whether the two can disagree like this, is a question for the class.

### Intersectionality

With two attributes, $A_1$ and $A_2$, a model with an interaction,

$$
Y = \gamma_1 A_1 + \gamma_2 A_2 + \delta A_1 A_2 + \dots ,
$$

gives the effect of $A_1$ as $\gamma_1$ when $A_2 = 0$ and
$\gamma_1 + \delta$ when $A_2 = 1$. A model without the interaction,
$\delta = 0$, assumes that the effect of one attribute is the same at
every level of the other: that being a woman has the same effect
whatever one's race, for example. Yang, Loftus and Stoyanovich build
causal models for intersectional fairness in which, in their words,
"we generally assume that f_j contains non-additive interactions
between sensitive attributes" (arXiv version, page 3), and keep main
effects and second-order interactions in their examples. In such a
model, each effect of one attribute is stated at a level of the other.

## Lenses

Who is in the data? Each driver is in the data once, with one value of
the attribute. The same driver with the other value, and $Y(1, M(0))$,
are in nobody's data: the model fills them in by abduction. A
counterfactual criterion is a statement about people the insurer has
never observed, and it is only as good as the model that supplies them.

You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. Which paths are fair;
which group is the baseline for the counterfactually fair premium, and
at what level; whether to price without the attribute, as the law
requires, or with it, as counterfactual fairness requires in the red
car world. The criteria compute the consequences of each choice and do
not make it.

What can be changed, and how? What things are considered "controlled
for" or "held fixed," and is that realistic? Abduction holds $U$ fixed
for the counterfactual driver, which assumes the model's $U$ is a
property of the person that would not change with the attribute. The
natural direct effect holds mileage at $M(0)$, a value no one is
observed at. Equal mileage in a regression is mileage held fixed in
the data, not by intervention, and the two differ when something else
drives both mileage and claims.

And why? An insurer prices on the variables it is allowed to use, and
the path-specific premium in the mileage world needs no sex at all. A
price that never mentions the attribute can still carry an indirect
effect that someone judged fair. Who judged it, and on what grounds?

## Readings

### Required

- Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan, *Fairness and Machine Learning:
  Limitations and Opportunities* (MIT Press, 2023),
  [chapter 5, Causality](https://fairmlbook.org/pdf/fairmlbook.pdf):
  "Graphical discrimination analysis" through the end of
  "Counterfactual discrimination analysis", pages 117 to 131 (printed
  page numbers; a PDF viewer shows them as 127 to 141). Direct effects,
  indirect paths, counterfactuals and Definition 5, quantitative path
  analysis, counterfactual discrimination criteria and counterfactuals
  in the law. The chapter writes $X$ for the treatment and $Z$ for the
  mediator.
- Re-read Loftus, *Modern Statistics 4 Data Science*,
  [section 3.4, Causality and ethics](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#causality-and-ethics):
  the red car, counterfactual fairness, shallow and deep
  counterfactuals, moral luck and path-specific counterfactual
  fairness.

### Optional

- The same book, chapter 5, "Validity of causal modeling" (pages 132
  to 137): whether categories such as race and gender can be variables
  in a causal model at all.
- The same book, chapter 4, "Tensions between the different views"
  through "The cost of fairness" (pages 85 to 92), which includes the
